speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apropos of what just happened, we do not hold you responsible for everything that happens in this House.
I was pointing out that the farmers want an individual plan. I was saying that I speak with some experience in this because I was present when the first crop insurance plan was put through. We found this difficult to sell to the farmer until one government, the government of Manitoba, sent out their field force to sit at the kitchen tables to explain to each individual farmer how he paid in, the government paid in, and the farmer got paid out. Now that crop insurance is widely accepted it is hard to believe it took 15 years before that acceptance came. I simply say that it is a futile use of the time of the members of this House to ask us to accept this bill when we know from experience that, if the farmers do not understand how the pay-out will occur, they will not sign up for it.
As a party you have a choice if you have this situation in front of you. We thought we could move in this House for a six months hoist which would have the effect of removing the bill from the House until the government could reconsider. In considering that you tend to ask yourself what it would accomplish. Will the government realize there has to be some form of cohesion in agricultural policy, and take this type of income stabilization legislation out of the hands of the minister in charge of the wheat board, who is too busy to look after the wheat board let alone look after this? Now that he is Minister of Transport he has no time for anything at all. I would go for a six months hoist if I thought the government would put this bill under the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) so that members of parliament could hold at least one minister responsible for what happens to agriculture.
It would save a lot of time if we showed our feelings by voting against the legislation at third reading. However, that is not very constructive unless you have some alternatives to put forward. What we have decided to do in this debate on third reading is to put forward as a party a series of three or maybe four proposals that are simple, easy to understand, and based on individual responsibility. At the same time they will help the government achieve what it wants.
The interest of the government in stabilization is simple. If farm income rises and falls in great cycles, when farm income is low the income of primary and secondary industry soon falls off and we get into a recession. Therefore from a monetary and fiscal point of view, it helps the government if you can have a stable income in this very valuable industry so that the tax take remains relatively constant.
Grain Stabilization
To give an example of the mathematics, if the government puts $2 into this fund, the farmer puts in $1, and payments out are made of the $3, that $3 goes through the system to the merchant, the transportation system, the manufacturers, and the primary industry. It has a multiplier effect of three. The $3 becomes $9 when you calculate the tax. If governments collect 40 per cent of the gross national product in tax, out of the $2 invested, the government gets back $3.60. That is the arithmetic of why governments want it.
Under the present plan the government will get back its $3.60 for sure, but the individual farmer does not know what he is going to get. He may get it when he does not want it. He may not get it when he needs it. Therefore it does not meet the farmer's test.
The proposals we are going to put forward meet the government's needs as well as the farmer's needs. These proposals will be made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) and, if he gets back, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) will make the third proposal. There is also one that I will make.
My proposal is elementary and simple. It is first that we allow a variable levy. This means that, instead of being a rigid 2 per cent, the farmer is allowed to pay anything up to 2 per cent or at whatever they set the levy. I say this for a reason. From the evidence given by the farmers, they would like to pay a lot more than 2 per cent in the good years so they can have the privilege of paying less in poorer years when they do not have the money.
The principle of a variable levy is workable. If a farmer wanted to contribute more or less than 2 per cent, that would be his business. The government contribution would be a variation, a proportion of what the farmer has paid. That would be a simple principle that the farmer can understand. If it averages out at 2 per cent, as the government calculates is necessary, the farmer will pay his share.
The second principle is that this plan entails individual accounting. With our present type computers we have the ability to record all the money in, the money out, the interest and so on, on an individual basis for every person in Canada. We do it for the Canadian farmer in the grain business through the wheat board on his shipments to the wheat board and the credits to him. We can do it also with this question of income stabilization.
The third principle is the triggering formula. I really do not care so much for this particular item, but if they want to have a triggering formula it has to be based on the individual. The government can get the gross income immediately from the Canadian Wheat Board and its other sources. It is not hard to establish the gross income. The expenses can be obtained from the income tax forms. The income tax people can do this very simply by tagging the forms to be looked at. This is available for every individual. It is entered into the account. If you want to take a figure for triggering and get the average net income over several years, it can be done. On an individual basis the computer can be programmed so there is no time lost.

December 11, 1975
Grain Stabilization
The fourth principle, and this is the important one, is that the individual alone decides when and to what extent he uses his individual fund. If he has had a series of good years and the fund is built up, and then he has a slight reduction below his average net income for five years, he does not have to take it unless he wants to take it. He himself decides what he wants to do with his averaging device. Likewise there might be a very bad year and he might want to take more out of the fund than would be normal if it were run by a regular formula. That is his business because, the fifth principle is when his own fund is exhausted, he draws down too much.
I do not believe the people of Canada should be asked to pay a subsidy to the farmer to stabilize his income. I think the farmer will accept that. He wants government off his back. He just wants a fair break. He wants his products sold. He wants to get an average price, a pool price, as they say, and he would like stability of income. But I do not think he expects the people of Canada to subsidize him in that regard. I would not be opposed, on this fifth principle of the program I am enunciating, to lending money to his fund, but he would have to pay interest on it, that is, if he wants to maintain the fund in a series of bad years.
I have put forward a simple, easily-understood type of proposal. It is actuarially sound. The individual decides how much he needs out of his own fund. If he doesn't take as much out as he needs, it is all his anyway. It is all credited to him. If he quits farming, it is there, available for him. Naturally he will pay income tax when he gets it, but the fact remains that the farmer individually is allowed to stabilize his own income.
Participation by the farmer and by the government is in the same proportion as in the bill before us. The government's interests are protected because if thousands of farmers experience a drop in income, a net drop over the whole area, the money would be paid out and go into circulation, and the government would get its taxes in the same way as usual. The interests of the farmer will be protected too, because he will know at all times that for every dollar he puts in he will get back three dollars. That is why he will buy the scheme.
It is in the interest of every Canadian to help this valuable industry stabilize its income, whether he works in a mine, or in the forest industry, or in a city. I say this because the chief sufferer and the chief beneficiary from variations in farm income is the person in other industries. I well recall in 1961, when we were in the recession of 1959 and 1960, there was a great influx of money from the sale of western wheat which pulled Canada out of the doldrums and set us on the longest period of growth this country has ever known, from 1961 to 1968. This was because the minute the farmer got his money he put it into circulation; it moved through the merchants and through secondary industry, the mines and the forests. As the head of the Bank of Canada at that time and as the minister of finance said at that time, this was the spark which brought Canada out of that recession.
I would like to see legislation of this type brought in. I would like to see a start made with a fund of this type.
This is how you keep the extra cost out of farming and how you protect the consumer against extra cost. If you stabilize a farmer's income you reduce his operating costs.
I put these views forward in very simple form as a bit of evidence that there is a constructive attitude on the part of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. We are not opposed to this legislation. We would just like to see the government pull this legislation out, keep the method of levies the same, keep the principle the same, but make the pay-out individual.
This doesn't mean anything, coming from me alone, unless I can bring evidence to show that this is the viewpoint of the farmers. We held five meetings of the standing committee in western Canada, and I am taking the evidence from two cities alone, Regina, on June 18, 1975, and Saskatoon on June 19, 1975. I am asking the government to note the source of the evidence. I am quoting from the deputy minister of agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan given on June 18, and reported at pages 12 and 13 of the Minutes of Proceedings. My question to Mr. Dalgliesh, the deputy minister, reads as follows:
My first question deals with your brief on page eight, headed off by the statement:
"The plan does not provide individual commodity or regional
income stability."
I would think this is the heart of the principle of this bill. This bill is an attempt on the part of the government to provide area stability to an industry, the whole Wheat Board area. You collect individually from the producers but the pay-out is for an area. My question specifically to you, is: in view of the difficulties we have had over the years with PFAA in trying to plan regions and boundaries, in view of the fact that farmers if they are going to accept this bill and go into it in large numbers and in view of the fact that we have had the experience of the crop insurance approach, whether the area approach or the individual approach is most attractive, would you think it would change this basic principle of the present bill to one of individual approach whereby the individual is allowed to decide whether he wants to go into the plan, and his gross income is easily ascertained, and where his expenses to the National Revenue Department are easily ascertained, we could have much wider acceptance on the part of individual farmers rather than on a complete Board area pay-out or block pay-out?
That is a long and complex question. Mr. Dalgliesh answered in this way:
You are really suggesting that the plan be amended to be on an individual producer basis; if there were 85,000 producers, there would be 85,000 individual programs, one for each individual producer.
At this point I interjected the words, "The same as crop insurance", and Mr. Dalgliesh went on to say:
Certainly, in concept I think the Saskatchewan government would agree that you do want to try to zero in to the individual producer because really that is the unit you are trying to stabilize. So, certainly, with that objective in mind, that would be desirable. I suppose the question would come in, in terms of ensuring that you were not stabilizing uneconomic production, you would want to make sure that that was not a factor and I think that might present some problems in the approach. I think you have to take some account of production in aggregate. If you stabilize the price for the commodities that he was producing and not put up the crop insurance to guarantee that the quantity of production was forthcoming, I would see the program being workable. Yes.
Now to the layman all this means that he is saying that in view of all the experience we have had, the bill before us

December 11, 1975

does not provide individual commodity or regional stability. He goes on to say that the best thing would be to work with the producers.
Now on the next page, page 13, I am quoting myself again, I was reported as saying:
That really winds up what I wanted to suggest. If we have crop insurance on an individual basis where you have a chance to insure up to a certain amount against the vicissitudes of weather, this gives us a chance on an individual basis, on a voluntary basis, to provide that same type of income protection or market protection, if you like, and with the other qualifications you have here, you have no objection.

I would conclude with one remark. I think this was the best representation we have had to date, in our four days out here, of an honest expression of farmers without any vested interest pressure on them. Thank you very much.
That was an extract from the final part of my questioning of Mr. Lemon, and all it adds up to, Mr. Speaker, is that the farmers of western Canada-other hon. members may bring additional evidence-spoke on every single occasion, as individuals, as groups, or as a government, in favour of the individual approach.
Grain Stabilization
When we came back to Ottawa to meet the minister, who did not go to the meetings to meet the farmers, I asked him whether he would consider positive, constructive proposals from the opposition. He replied: "No; the government has decided this is the way the bill is, and the only amendments we will accept are on four or five minor points brought in by the Federation of Agriculture". In face of this evidence the minister deliberately turned down the request of the farmers of the west who were willing to pay into the fund if they knew how they would get their money out. But no, the minister said the government had already decided. I do not believe the government as a whole ever decided anything. I think it was the minister who decided that he was not going to change, regardless of what the farmers or the opposition said.
So we are faced, Mr. Speaker, with a bill that (a) is not going to be accepted by the farmers, and (b) is going to be forced on the farmers by the minister in the face of their objections. Because this proposal is essentially voluntary, even though the legislation is complicated, I say here and now that the legislation is not going to be accepted by even 10 per cent of our farmers.
There is one group of farmers for whom I want to put in a plea. I know that the older farmers look forward to retirement in the next ten years and they are not so concerned with stabilizing their incomes between now and then. But the young farmers in their late twenties and early thirties who are operating under a huge debt because they are buying land, equipment, and the livestock needed to make an income, desperately want some form of stabilization of income. The reason I so much wanted this bill altered was that these farmers could have stabilization of income while at the same time a sufficient number of farmers were brought into the fund to create stability, thus achieving what the government wanted, and making more certain that young farmers would be protected by a large and available fund.
I have spoken at great length, Mr. Speaker, on the individual approach to income stabilization, and because this is such a serious matter for the western farmers I want to make it very clear that there are alternatives. I say this bill will not be acceptable. Whether we throw it out tonight on a six months' hoist or we vote it out makes no difference. It all depends on the government. If the government really wants to help the western farmers it can withdraw the legislation, amend it, and bring it in again, incorporating one of these simple alternatives that we are prepared to offer. But if the government wants to ram it through regardless of the feelings of the farmers and the opposition, then it has to be willing to pay the price, and the price it will have to pay is continued antagonism toward the government on the part of the farmers of western Canada.
I do not think it is any secret that the government has tried its level best to make the farmers of western Canada love it. But every move the government makes seems to cause more antagonism. I believe one of the reasons for this is the government's failure to realize that the Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Alberta farmers are not ignorant peasants of the last century. They are young, sophisticated, modern businessmen who know exactly what they are trying to do, and who can figure out the pros and cons

December 11, 1975
Grain Stabilization
of any given program. In general they would like to have income stabilization, but they are not going to take on something when they do not know what the payout is.
If the government is really sincere in trying to put an income stabilization plan into effect, let the government make changes. However, I suggest that so long as the matter is in the hands of the present minister in charge of the Wheat Board we will not get these changes made. He is determined to have his own way regardless of what the farmers or the opposition think. Those who sat on the committee with us during the last three years know that the opposition have made constructive proposals. Over and over again the Minister of Agriculture has accepted our proposals and the result has been better legislation. All members of the standing committee know this to be true. But the minute we meet up with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, all we get is his black and white inflexibility.
If the government wants a favourable movement among the farmers of the west, for heaven's sakes let it put agriculture under one minister who at least is willing to listen. After all, we are not all bad on this side. As I say, we have put forward positive suggestions. When a minister accepts them, we stand up in the House and support legislation. I stood up and supported the minister on one occasion in this session, but members on this side disagreed with me. However, that is the agreement we made in committee.
We have tried to push things forward on a constructive basis in order to help agriculture. This is not something you kick around from a partisan point of view, and this is why I plead with members who sit on the government side to put pressure on the cabinet if they have any influence at all. How about working for the farmers for once, and get the government to put agriculture under one minister? Then we will try to help the minister achieve a better agricultural industry.
We need agricultural stabilization and stabilization of agricultural incomes, and I should like to see this applied not only in respect of the farmers growing grain in western Canada, but later on in respect of the livestock industry and farmers all across this country. But it will have to be on an individual basis in order to work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate at third reading with a view to agreeing with much of what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has said. That should indicate something to the government. In view of the rare occasions the NDP and the Conservatives agree on anything, there must be something to this.
Members of the official opposition and of this party tried without success to get amendments to this legislation accepted in the committee. The government did accept a couple of minor changes which resulted in slight improvements to the bill, but government members were adamant, stubborn, as well as ignorant about accepting some other fundamental changes to the legislation which would not have detracted from or destroyed the principle. They

refused to accept these amendments, and as a result the legislation is still bad and terribly deficient.
Some four years ago the Liberal government had the views of farm organizations, the three western provincial governments, as well as members of the opposition on what a grain stabilization program should be. It was expressed at that time that a grain stabilization program should not only be for the benefit of grain farmers but as well for the livestock producers and the growers of other products, including the farmers of the sea-the fishermen. Four years later the government still remains stubborn and ignorant, and still refuses to produce legislation which conforms with the principles of a stabilization program that will stabilize farm incomes involving a variety of products.
The original program laid before the government four years ago has seen many technical revisions, as in this bill. While I agree that the government did accept two of the submissions of the opposition four years ago, it has not complied with the principle. The government did accept the idea that the bill had to be based on net income rather than gross income. This was a 180 degree turn-around by the government.
The plan we now have before us is as abstract in principle as the original bill. It does not seek to stabilize the price of grain and it does not stabilize or guarantee the incomes of the producers. One of the most exasperating aspects of the bill is that it is next to impossible to detect the rationale behind it, and this lack of rationale, together with the extreme complexity of the bill, is what everyone complains about. Even government members admitted it is difficult to comprehend. This makes any attempt at explaining the bill to the farmers an exercise in frustration.
A paper released by the minister on September 4, 1974, lists four objectives for the grain stabilization plan. I should like to comment on each of them.
The first objective the minister outlined was to protect grain producers in the designated area from uncertainty and variation in returns due to temporary market fluctuations. Further on in his paper the minister used the expression "it transforms uncertainty into insurable risk". On page 10 of the minister's paper it is stated:
-the government has stated that the plan has to operate within a level that is actuarially sound. The level set by the government is 6 per cent of gross receipts from commercial grain production, with the government paying % and producers paying Vi.
It is obvious that the plan is being portrayed in the minister's statement as an income insurance scheme, but in reality it is not. In reality payments will be made by the grain stabilization fund if the proceeds from the sale of a proportion of the prairie grain crop in any year falls below the average proceeds in the previous five-year period, after adjustments have been made for changes in certain, but by no means all, expenses incurred in production and sale of the grain. In that event participating farmers will receive payments proportionate to their contributions. Whether individual farmers actually suffer declines in receipts or income is immaterial under this plan.
It seems to me that the proposed stabilization plan is being portrayed as an insurance scheme and, since it is a contributory plan, farmers should know what insurance
December 11, 1975

they are buying; in other words, the plan must relate to the needs of individuals. It should be possible for individuals to determine what benefits would accrue t( them if the event against which they are insuring themselves should occur. That surely is a cardinal principle of all insurance plans whether they are private, mixed private and social such as crop insurance, or universal social insurance schemes such as workmen's compensation, unemployment insurance, hospital or medical insurance.
A second cardinal principle of all such schemes is that indemnities are paid to those who experience the ill effects of the event against which the plan provides insurance, and not to others. The proposed stabilization act sins against both these principles. In fact the bill completely ignores them.
A farmer who insures his crop with the Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta crop insurance plans knows what he insures himself for; he knows to what level he is indemnified if his yield falls below the insured level. A worker who pays unemployment insurance knows what he may expect in benefits in the event he loses his job and fails to find another. That is as it should be. In contrast, a person participating in the proposed prairie grain stabilization plan has no way of knowing when he will receive benefits, how much he will receive, or whether he will receive benefits when he really needs them. That is a complete betrayal of the principles enunciated by the minister in his statement.
In the three prairie provinces crop insurance will only indemnify those insured farmers who suffer specified losses, but will make no payments to all insured farmers because the over-all yield in the province may be below the five-year average. Similarly the Unemployment Insurance Commission will pay benefits to insured persons who lose their jobs, but will not make payments to all those making unemployment insurance contributions on the basis that there is a slack in the economy. Yet that is precisely what Bill C-41 proposes to do.
If the Manitoba crop insurance program operated on the same basis, as the minister, his deputy, and the Manitoba Crop Insurance Board told the committee, it could conceivably have taken the $8.2 million paid in indemnities in 1974 and distributed it to the insured farmers on the basis of their premium contributions. It is quite possible then that farmers with very high yields would have received large payments and the farmers with partial or total crop losses would have received far less.
I am sorry the minister is not here since this is his bill. I appreciate why he was not here when the bill was called at the report stage. He had a very important prior commitment to speak to the Alberta Wheat Pool. What I find passing strange is how disorganized that government is over there, shown by the fact that the government House leader would call a bill on a day on which the minister responsible had to be absent. If that is not sloppy handling I have never seen it.
If the minister is at the cabinet meeting advising the government to treat the postal workers in the same way he has advised the government to treat the farmers in this bill, it would be much better if he were in the House for
Grain Stabilization
the debate on this bill. At least then we could keep our eyes on him. If we were to operate the unemployment insurance-Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman across the way who is yelling had got up today to speak on behalf of the veterans, especially since he is the chairman of the committee, he might have made a contribution, but he did not have the guts to do so. He just sat there like a sheep when the vote was being taken.
As an indication of how ridiculous this bill is and how it completely perverts the principle of stabilizing incomes whether in respect of grain or anything else, if the Unemployment Insurance Commission were operated on the same principles as Bill C-41 what would happen is that the Unemployment Insurance Commission would calculate for all of Canada the average annual bill for wages and salaries on which unemployment insurance contributions are made. They would adjust it for the changes in the number of unemployment insurance contributors and for certain changes in the consumer price index, and if the adjusted total wage bill fell below the average of the previous five years, the Unemployment Insurance Commission would make a payment to all wage and salary earners. Each would be paid proportionate to his contributions. Those who had paid the maximum would receive the greatest payment. Those who had paid the lowest premium would receive the lowest payment. The unemployed person who had made little or no contributions would receive little or nothing.
I doubt, and the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, as well as many farmers doubt that this kind of a proposal to stabilize the net proceeds from wages and salaries in Canada would meet with the approval of the Canadian people. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, trying to operate the UIC on the basis proposed by this bill? If the unemployment insurance program were operated on the basis this bill proposes, the fellow who worked all year around and made UIC contributions would receive the highest payment from the fund, and the fellow who was laid off for four months and did not contribute to the fund during those four months would receive the lowest payment, or no payment at all. That is what this bill proposes.
The bill rewards the fortunate and penalizes the unfortunate. The farmer who makes the highest contribution to the fund in a year of pay-out receives the highest payment. If that is not backward in respect of any kind of insurance or stabilization plan, I do not know what is. If the national hospitalization program were operated on the same basis the people would pay their premiums, the government would compute the total bill for hospital care in the country, and in a year in which hospital care exceeded the previous five-year average everybody who paid a premium would receive a payment whether or not they had been in hospital. That has to be some kind of perversion of any kind of stabilization plan.
The more we deal with this bill the more convinced I am that it is still a bad bill. It is almost as bad as the legislation of 1971, which is saying something. It is obvious so far as the individual farmer is concerned that the plan does not meet the objective of the minister which is contained in his statement to the effect that the plan would transform uncertainty into insurable risk.

December 11, 1975
Adjournment Debate
The second objective listed by the minister was to:
... ensure that growth and development of the grain sector is consistent with basic market forces and that the grain sector develops in a manner consistent with competitive advantage in world grain markets.
While the relevance of this statement escapes me, I am disturbed over the policy implications that would seem to flow from that kind of philosophy. In effect the statement seems to suggest that there should be no stability if basic market forces dictate that there should be instability. The expression that the grain sector should develop "in a manner consistent with competitive advantage in world grain markets" I submit is entirely out of tune with recent international events, including the efforts by the Government of Canada to arrive at a better planned, more orderly world food distribution system.
Concepts such as world food banks, international commodity agreements, and the new economic order insisted upon by the developing nations are incompatible with the 19th century philosophy of competitive advantage. Moreover, that philosophy is the exact opposite, I remind the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), to the basic competitive advantage and the two-price Wheat Act enacted by the House of Commons recently.
The legislation betrays much of what the government has said, not to mention betraying the grain producer of Canada, the principle of income insurance and income stability, as well as income stabilization, or whatever one might like to call it. Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-CRITERIA USED IN AWARDING CONTRACT FOR STAMP MEDALLION TO JACQUES CARTIER MINT
OLYMPIC GAMES-CRITERIA USED IN AWARDING CONTRACT FOR STAMP MEDALLION TO JACQUES CARTIER MINT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to bother the postal department at this crucial time of indecision between the department, the government, and the Anti-Inflation Board. However, when I put my question to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mack-asey) on December 2, the question which we have an opportunity to air tonight, it was of course assumed at that time that the postal problems were solved at least for a longer temporary period than the week or so that has elapsed since then.
Be that as it may, the purpose of my question is simply to find the criteria which led the Post Office to award the Olympic stamp medallion contract to the Jacques Cartier Mint, of which Mr. Norton Cooper is the president, and which is a subsidiary of Silver Shield Mines Limited. The reason I feel we have the right to know the department's decision in this regard is the fact that in November of 1972 charges were laid against the same Norton Cooper, president of Silver Shield Mines Incorporated.

Also, officials of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion were charged and subsequently convicted as a result of bribes being offered by Mr. Cooper to DREE employees for the purpose of having Silver Shield Mines Incorporated obtain a federal government grant. The DREE grant in the amount of nearly three-quarters of a million dollars was later withdrawn and the DREE officials in question suspended, because as the then deputy minister in charge of DREE, Mr. J. D. Love, said:
An officer in a responsible federal government position was offered and received improper benefits from a person or persons associated with Silver Shield and its subsidiary Jacques Cartier Mint.
Subsequently Norton Cooper proceeded to plan to take legal action against DREE for withdrawing the grant.
On June 8 the federal government awarded Mr. Cooper a contract, number 69C74, for the purpose of minting stamp medallions. On June 27, 1974, Norton Cooper was convicted. As a result, on January 30, 1975, the Post Office Department decided to rewrite the original contract and awarded the new contract to Jacques Cartier Mint-contract number 108C74.
Regardless of any internal changes within Jacques Cartier Mint regarding its directors, the fact remains that Norton Cooper, who is willing to sue the federal government, who is responsible for the suspension and ultimate conviction of federal government officials-Norton Cooper who himself has been convicted of bribery for the purpose of obtaining federal financial assistance, is the same Norton Cooper who today finds himself with yet another lucrative government contract, not to mention the fact that Joseph Zappia, who is the head of the consortium building the Olympic village-who happens to have under his belt a contract for minting Olympic medallions in Switzerland- who has been the subject of recent RCMP raids on his offices and private dwelling, is the Joseph Zappia who is connected with Norton Cooper by way of having the contract of packaging the medal stamps that Cooper's company is minting.
This is just a small example of the background of yet two more shady characters who continue to be able to deal with the government which, in simple terms, is either naive itself or at least just as shady, to say the least.
In these days of uncertainties and questionable practices within the government and its agencies, whether it be the Post Office, Air Canada, or the countless areas dealing with public funds surfacing as near scandalous, one would assume that the Post Office Department would be far more careful as to how and to whom government contracts are awarded. I do not have to repeat that I am one who supports the Olympic ideal wholeheartedly, but I believe that one of the reasons that financially and otherwise the staging of the Olympics in Montreal is encountering the great difficulties that we are all aware of, is there exists a multitude of unbusiness like, improper, and shady practices.
That is why I believe it is imperative for the Post Office Department to come up with an answer to my original question as to what criteria led them to award yet another non-tendered contract, this time to Jacques Cartier Mint.
December 11, 1975

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-CRITERIA USED IN AWARDING CONTRACT FOR STAMP MEDALLION TO JACQUES CARTIER MINT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern about our problem in the Post Office at present but I assure him that the moment of decision has arrived. I hope that we will have an announcement in the next short while about where we are going, certainly by tomorrow.
I would also say that the hon. member is correct in his chronology of events up to a certain point, but he failed to mention that Mr. Norton Cooper is no longer an officer of the Jacques Cartier Mint.
I would like to inform the hon. member that contract No. 108C74 was awarded to Jacques Cartier Mint on January 20, 1975. Of course, as I indicated earlier, Mr. Norton Cooper is no longer a director of the said company. A total of eight companies were asked to submit tenders, but only two responded, and Jacques Cartier Mint was the bid that qualified for the said contract on the basis of a quality product. A qualitative analysis of the bids was made in consultation with the Department of Supply and Services and the Royal Canadian Mint.
We would like to underline the fact that the Department of Justice was consulted on the legal aspects of this matter, and the Post Office Department was advised that nothing could be done but to award the contract to Jacques Cartier Mint, with the proviso that the company be advised that Mr. Norton Cooper could not benefit from the contract.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SURPLUS OF SKIM MILK POWDER-SUGGESTED USE IN FOOD AID PROGRAMS
AGRICULTURE-SURPLUS OF SKIM MILK POWDER-SUGGESTED USE IN FOOD AID PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate once again in the adjournment debate this evening. I believe it is the second time in as many weeks.
My deep concern tonight is shared by my colleagues, the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis), the hon. member for Huron-Middlesex (Mr. McKinley), the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), and many others on this side of the House. This deep concern is over the recent reduction of subsidy payments by the government to industrial milk producers.
My concern over the present high level of stocks of skim milk powder that are reported to be triple those of last year, and my awareness of the great need and usefulness of skim milk powder for the world food aid program prompted me to raise the following question on December 3, as reported at page 9680 of Hansard:
As stocks of skim milk powder on hand this year are three times larger than last year's, being 300 million pounds, compared with approximately 100 million pounds, and as CIDA bought less skim milk this year than last, has the Minister of Agriculture made representations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or to CIDA directly, in the hope that additional volumes of this product will be purchased for world food aid?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) replied-and in part he said-yes, we have done that, we have asked the head of the Canadian Dairy Commission and our trade officers to explore every possible avenue for the sale of
Adjournment Debate
skim milk powder. He indicated also that the world surpluses of skim milk powder are larger than ever and that the distribution problem is even greater than before. Although I appreciate that information I must point out that I am fully aware of the existence of those conditions. In fact my colleague, the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot, will touch on one of the reasons for this condition later this evening.
The minister had admitted that discussions along these lines have been held, but let us examine the results. CIDA's purchase of skim milk powder for the world food program for the fiscal year 1972-73 was 25.5 million pounds; for 1973-74, it was 23.6 million pounds, and in 1974-75, 23.9 million pounds were purchased. But CIDA's purchase for this fiscal year of 1975-76 is only 14 million pounds.
At a time when our domestic stocks are in a position of extreme surplus it is unacceptable to learn that our commitment has been reduced by almost one half. I am certain that most Canadians would agree that the need for world food aid has drastically increased over the past ten years.
Canada's current commitment of skim milk powder through CIDA for aid is 13A of a million pounds less than our last ten year average.
I do not want to belittle Canada's contribution for indeed in total it is sizeable-4,000 tons of wheat, $5 million in canned beef, $l'/2 million in fish, and $1 million for beans, in addition to the reduced amount of skim milk powder. I do want to make it perfectly clear that what I am asking for is a greater commitment by the government to the world food program by an increased utilization of skim milk powder.
The government dodges the problem by pointing to present world surpluses. It excuses itself for the lack of success in export sales because of our poor comparitive position which results from the fact, Mr. Speaker, that the government does not support certain dairy products to the extent that they are supported by our foreign competitors.
I want to emphasize that shipments of skim milk powder to the world food aid program are not subject to competition in the world market place. Our commitment is a domestic matter-a local decision made by the government. Thus the amount of food that goes into our foreign aid basket is completely under the control of our own authorities.
I ask the government, and particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), and the Minister of Agriculture, at a time when domestic stocks are at their current level, when our present commitment is only about one half that of the previous two years, and at a time when the need for world food aid is urgent and pressing-I ask that they take prompt action to triple the volume of skim milk powder being placed into the world food aid program. I am certain that it would be accepted gratefully and with open arms. A greater percentage of the world's hungry could be fed; Canada would come closer to fulfilling her obligation in this area, and Canadians would experience a greater sense of satisfaction and pride.

December 11, 1975
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-COMPREHENSIVE MILK MARKETING PLAN-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT AMENDED TO PERMIT INCREASED CHEESE IMPORTS
AGRICULTURE-COMPREHENSIVE MILK MARKETING PLAN-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT AMENDED TO PERMIT INCREASED CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), the hon. member for Huron-Middlesex (Mr. McKinley), and I have been asking

questions regarding the government's industrial milk policy, and tonight I wish to deal with one aspect of that problem.
For almost five years there has been in existence a written agreement which has been commonly called the comprehensive milk marketing plan It was signed by the Canadian Dairy Commission on behalf of the federal government, and by various provincial government marketing authorities and provincial producer marketing boards. The purpose of the plan is to manage the supply of Canadian milk by means of quotas in order to provide a balance between the domestic supply of butterfat and the requirements of the Canadian market for butterfat in manufactured dairy products, plus commercial exports. It has been made very clear that the purpose of the plan is not to restrict development of our dairy industry. On the contrary, the agreement should operate to promote sales of dairy products at home and abroad. The quotas are designed only to manage the total dairy production, to ensure that there is an effective market for that production.
In April, 1975, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said we may have to continue to import some butter, but then went on to say:
However, domestic consumption will continue to be met predominantly by Canadian production.
This, of course, is consistent with the comprehensive milk marketing plan.
Then came the shock of the Minister of Agriculture's statement of November 4, and I quote the pertinent paragraph:
In accordance with the decision of April 18, 1975, imports will be allowed to increase gradually over the next several years until they reach not less than the equivalent of 10 per cent of manufactured products. The current (cheese) import quota of 50 million pounds represents 5 per cent of total Canadian consumption of manufactured dairy products. The size of the next year's quota will be established shortly.
First, and obviously, the decision to permit an increase to at least 10 per cent of our market was not in accordance with the April, 1975, statement. In my view, and in the opinion of milk producers, it is just the opposite.
Secondly, I submit that this decision is a clear contravention of the federal-provincial agreement. The agreement's purpose is to balance Canadian milk supply with domestic and export demands for our dairy products. How can this possibly be balanced when we give away a minimum of 10 per cent of our domestic market to producers and processors in foreign countries?
I do not know what happened between April and November this year and possibly I will never find out, but I can only conclude that, once again, Canadian agriculture has been sold down the river at the bargaining table for international trade.
This brings me to my third point. I submit that this sell-out constituted another breach of the federal-provincial agreement. There is a clear provision, and I believe it is in Section 13, that no order or regulation bearing on the provisions and purposes of the plan shall be made without, first, prior notification to the other parties, and secondly, concurrence by the other parties that such change does not contravene the purposes and provisions of the plan.
December 11, 1975

Clearly there has been no concurrence by the provincial producer groups and, what is even worse, I believe that there was no notification whatsoever. I specifically asked the minister in the House of Commons on December 9 if he had notified these other groups, and I quote his reply:
We had many discussions with them. I am not sure whether or not that was discussed, but I am sure that they knew and were well aware of the increased importation into Canada of industrial cheese at that time. They made strong representations against this and they are making strong representations against this at present. We are reconsidering the whole situation.
All I can say is that the government darn well better reconsider. It is clear that the minister did not have provincial concurrence; in fact he expressly states he has just the opposite, and secondly I have a written statement form one provincial producer group which says in part as follows:
At no time during the current dairy year have the representatives of the federal government notified the signatory parties to the plan that the federal government wanted the definition of what constitutes Canada's industrial milk requirements changed.
Canadian producers are well able to supply the domestic market. As a matter of fact they are now being penalized because we allegedly have too much milk. 1 remember well just two years ago the government's alarm because milk production was falling. Now the government says we are going to take away at least 10 per cent of your market and give it to foreign producers. How in heaven's name can any milk producer plan intelligently for the future when he is being overwhelmed with almost monthly changes in government policy?
On the one hand we have subsidy reductions which for three of my typical milk producers resulted in reduced incomes for September production of $330.85, $278, and $211 respectively. By year end these losses will range from $1,477 to $2,647.55.
On the other hand we now have an annual cheese import quota of 50 million pounds which costs Canadian producers approximately $18 million, or $360,000 for every million pounds of imported cheese. I also strongly suggest that foreign governments are subsidizing, directly or indirectly, these products which put our Canadian producers in a very difficult, if not impossible, competitive position. Our Canadian cheddar is the best in the world, and we have developed an excellent line of specialty cheeses in recent years, which should be given a fair chance in our domestic market, and hopefully in export markets as well.
The minister has told me he will reconsider this whole problem. I beg him to do so immediately because Canadian farmers, at this very moment, are feeling that again their products have been used as pawns in international trade arrangements.
If the minister wants to know what some farmers are saying let me read a postscript to a letter I recently received from a dairyman:
In fact what farmers are really protesting is a wage decrease while other professions insist on a substantial increase.
Adjournment Debate
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I wish to read a letter that is being forwarded today by my office to the Minister of Agriculture, other ministers who are involved in the problem, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the Canadian Dairy Commission. It is as follows:
The members of Perth County Milk Committee, who represent the most producers who produce the most milk of any county in Ontario, would like to express deep concern-

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-COMPREHENSIVE MILK MARKETING PLAN-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT AMENDED TO PERMIT INCREASED CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is not here. In his absence I have undertaken to answer the hon. member's question. I can sympathize a great deal, I may say, with the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) and the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise). Tomorrow I have to face a group of dairy farmers who are also very concerned about this matter. The answer I have to make will not be very satisfying to anyone. Nevertheless, I think the hon. member has partly answered the question himself by drawing attention to the tremendous surpluses of skimmed milk powder which are held around the world. I believe the surplus in Europe right now is a million tons.
The comprehensive milk marketing plan is an agreement under which returns from export sales of skimmed milk powder and domestic sales are equalized. This is accomplished by means of a levy against producer market returns which is used by the Canadian Dairy Commission to assist exports of skimmed milk powder.
The second major objective of the plan is to balance supply with the requirements of the market, on a butterfat basis. The balance takes account of exports, primarily cheese and at the time the agreement was made, imports of cheese and butter accounted for a significant percentage of requirements.
The management committee which is composed of the heads of provincial milk marketing agencies, and which is chaired by the Canadian Dairy Commission, has continuously examined demand and supply.
The statistics which have been used by the management committee included the figure for the actual imports of cheese into Canada for each of the past several years. The management committee was aware that under the import policy existing up to the middle of this year, imports were not restricted in terms of quantity but by end-use. The government moved quickly to put quantitative restrictions on the total of cheese imports when it became evident that imports in 1975 would rise more than in the preceding years. The level of this quantitative restriction is now being reviewed by the government.
